explanation: A cerebellopontine angle tumor (typically acoustic/vestibular schwannoma) affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) causing hearing loss and vertigo, and CN VII (facial) causing facial paralysis. These nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle.
keyConcept: Cerebellopontine angle tumor: affects CN VII (facial) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear).
modelAnswer: Facial nerve (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). These cranial nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle and are commonly affected by acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas).

explanation: Four structures wind around the cerebral peduncle: optic tract (lateral), trochlear nerve (lateral, emerges dorsally), posterior cerebral artery (lateral), and basal vein (dorsal). The cerebral peduncle is the ventral part of the midbrain.
keyConcept: Structures around cerebral peduncle: optic tract, trochlear nerve, PCA, basal vein.
modelAnswer: Optic tract (wraps around the posterolateral aspect), trochlear nerve (CN IV - emerges just below the inferior colliculus and winds around the peduncle), posterior cerebral artery (on the superior surface), and basal vein (dorsal aspect).

explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded anteriorly by the optic chiasma, anterolaterally by the optic tract, posterolaterally by the cerebral peduncle, and posteriorly by the upper border of the pons. The floor is the posterior perforated substance.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa: anterior = optic chiasma; lateral = optic tract; posterolateral = cerebral peduncle; posterior = upper pons.
modelAnswer: Anteriorly: optic chiasma. Anterolaterally: optic tract. Posterolaterally: cerebral peduncle. Posteriorly: upper border of pons. The floor is formed by the posterior perforated substance.

explanation: The contents of the interpeduncular fossa include the tuber cinereum (hypothalamic eminence), mammillary bodies (posterior), posterior perforated substance (vascular area), and the oculomotor nerve emerges from the medial side of the cerebral peduncle.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa contents: tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, CN III.
modelAnswer: Tuber cinereum (hypothalamic eminence), mammillary bodies (part of Papez circuit), posterior perforated substance (contains central branches of posterior cerebral artery), and the oculomotor nerve (emerges between cerebral peduncles).

explanation: The three elevations seen on the posterior surface of the lower closed medulla are the gracile tubercle (medial, for lower limb), cuneate tubercle (lateral, for upper limb), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (forming the lateral boundary). These overlie the respective nuclei.
keyConcept: Posterior medulla elevations: gracile tubercle, cuneate tubercle, ICP. Correspond to dorsal column nuclei.
modelAnswer: Gracile tubercle (medial, contains gracile nucleus for lower limb proprioception), cuneate tubercle (lateral, contains cuneate nucleus for upper limb proprioception), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (forms the posterolateral boundary of the medulla).

explanation: The open medulla has the following borders: base = the medullary stria ( fibers crossing to cerebellum), apex = continuous with the cerebral aqueduct above and central canal below, floor = hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular area.
keyConcept: Open medulla borders: base = stria; apex = aqueduct/canal; floor = hypoglossal/vagal/vestibular trigones.
modelAnswer: Base: medullary stria (transverse fibers crossing to cerebellum). Apex: continuous superiorly with cerebral aqueduct and inferiorly with central canal. Floor: hypoglossal trigone (overlies hypoglossal nucleus), vagal trigone (overlies dorsal vagal nucleus), and vestibular area (vestibular nuclei).

explanation: The posterior surface of the pons has: base = medullary stria (transverse pontine fibers entering the cerebellum), apex = continuous with cerebral aqueduct, floor = medial eminence, facial colliculus (facial nerve wrapping around abducent nucleus), and vestibular area.
keyConcept: Posterior pons: stria at base, aqueduct at apex, floor has eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area.
modelAnswer: Base: medullary stria ( transverse pontine fibers). Apex: continuous with cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius. Floor: medial eminence (contains corticospinal fibers), facial colliculus ( CN VI nucleus with CN VII fibers looping around it), and vestibular area (vestibular nuclei).

explanation: The posterior surface of the midbrain shows the corpora quadrigemina - two superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (auditory relay). These are separated by a cross-shaped sulcus. The cerebral peduncles are visible ventrally.
keyConcept: Midbrain posterior features: 4 colliculi (2 superior, 2 inferior) - visual and auditory centers.
modelAnswer: Four colliculi: two superior colliculi (visual reflexes - part of visual pathway, coordinates head/eye movements) and two inferior colliculi (auditory relay - part of lateral lemniscus pathway). They form the quadrigeminal plate separated by a cruciform sulcus.

explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle is formed superiorly by the superior cerebellar peduncles and superior medullary velum (containing the trochlear decussation), and inferiorly by the inferior medullary velum and the choroid plexus.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior = superior cerebellar peduncle + superior medullary velum; inferior = inferior medullary velum.
modelAnswer: Superiorly: superior cerebellar peduncle and superior medullary velum (form the upper roof). Inferiorly: inferior medullary velum (forms the lower roof). The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle lies in the lower part of the roof.

explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle has two parts: pontine part (upper) showing medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; and medullary part (lower) showing hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle floor: pontine = eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area; medullary = hypoglossal/vagal/vestibular trigones.
modelAnswer: Pontine part: medial eminence, facial colliculus (CN VI nucleus with CN VII fibers), and vestibular area (vestibular nuclei). Medullary part: hypoglossal trigone (over hypoglossal nucleus), vagal trigone (over dorsal vagal nucleus), and vestibular trigone (vestibular nuclei).

explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle are: superiorly = the superior cerebellar peduncle; inferiorly = the inferior cerebellar peduncle plus the gracile and cuneate tracts; laterally = the lateral recess (extending toward the cerebellum).
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle lateral boundaries: superior = SCP, inferior = ICP + gracile/cuneate tracts, lateral recess.
modelAnswer: Superiorly: superior cerebellar peduncle. Inferiorly: inferior cerebellar peduncle and the gracile and cuneate tracts. The lateral boundary also includes the lateral recess, which extends toward the cerebellopontine angle.

explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle lies in the lower part of the roof (inferiorly), protruding through the lateral recesses. It is formed by the tela choroidea and is continuous with the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles via the foramen of Luschka.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle choroid plexus: lower part of roof, in tela choroidea of inferior roof.
modelAnswer: Lower (inferior) part of the roof of the fourth ventricle. The choroid plexus is formed by the tela choroidea (pia mater + ependyma) and protrudes through the lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka).

explanation: The GSE (general somatic efferent) cranial nerve nuclei are: oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII). These supply extraocular muscles and tongue muscles.
keyConcept: GSE cranial nerve nuclei: CN III, IV, VI, XII. Supply extraocular and tongue muscles.
modelAnswer: Nucleus of oculomotor nerve (CN III), nucleus of trochlear nerve (CN IV), nucleus of abducent nerve (CN VI), and nucleus of hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). These supply the extraocular muscles (except superior oblique and lateral rectus) and tongue muscles.

explanation: The SVE (special visceral efferent) nuclei include: motor nucleus of CN V (muscles of mastication + tensor tympani/palate), motor nucleus of CN VII (facial muscles), and nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI - pharynx/larynx muscles).
keyConcept: SVE nuclei: motor V (mastication), motor VII (facial expression), nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI - pharynx/larynx).
modelAnswer: Motor nucleus of trigeminal (CN V): supplies muscles of first pharyngeal arch (masticatory muscles, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, anterior digastric). Motor nucleus of facial (CN VII): supplies muscles of second pharyngeal arch (facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric). Nucleus ambiguus: CN IX - stylopharyngeus; CN X and XI - muscles of palate, pharynx, and larynx.

explanation: The GVE (general visceral efferent) nuclei include: Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III - pupillary constriction), superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII - lacrimal and salivary glands), inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX - parotid gland), and dorsal vagal nucleus (CN X - thoracic/abdominal viscera).
keyConcept: GVE nuclei: Edinger-Westphal (III), superior salivatory (VII), inferior salivatory (IX), dorsal vagal (X).
modelAnswer: Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III) - parasympathetic to eye (pupillary constriction, accommodation). Superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII) - submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, lacrimal gland. Inferior salivatory nucleus (CN IX) - parotid gland. Dorsal vagal nucleus (CN X) - parasympathetic to thoracic and abdominal viscera.

explanation: The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. These are muscles of the neck and shoulder that control head movement and scapular elevation.
keyConcept: Accessory nerve (spinal part): supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Purely motor.
modelAnswer: Sternomastoid muscle (rotates head to opposite side) and trapezius muscle (elevates scapula, rotates head). These are the only two muscles supplied by the spinal part of the accessory nerve.

explanation: The spinal part of the accessory nerve originates from the spinal nucleus located in the ventral (anterior) horn of the upper 5 cervical segments (C1-C5) of the spinal cord. The fibers ascend through the foramen magnum to join the cranial root.
keyConcept: Accessory nerve spinal root: ventral horns of C1-C5. Ascends through foramen magnum.
modelAnswer: Spinal nucleus located in the ventral horn of the upper five cervical segments of the spinal cord (C1-C5). The axons ascend through the vertebral canal, enter the skull via the foramen magnum, and join the cranial root to form the complete accessory nerve.

explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal supplies the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoids) and four non-mastication muscles: tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric.
keyConcept: Motor V: 4 mastication muscles + tensor tympani, tensor palate, mylohyoid, anterior digastric.
modelAnswer: The four muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid) plus tensor tympani (in middle ear), tensor veli palatini (palate), mylohyoid (floor of mouth), and anterior belly of digastric (suprahyoid).

explanation: The medulla is supplied by: anterior spinal artery (medial medulla), posterior inferior cerebellar artery (lateral medulla), direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, and posterior spinal artery (posterior surface).
keyConcept: Medulla blood supply: anterior spinal, PICA, vertebral artery branches, posterior spinal artery.
modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery (supplies medial medulla including pyramids and hypoglossal nucleus), posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA - supplies lateral medulla including vestibular nuclei and cerebellum), medullary branches of vertebral artery, and posterior spinal artery (supplies posterior medulla).

explanation: The pons is supplied by branches of the basilar artery, which runs in the basilar groove on the anterior surface. These include pontine arteries that penetrate the pons to supply the pontine nuclei and tegmentum.
keyConcept: Pons: supplied by branches of basilar artery. Multiple pontine arteries penetrate the pons.
modelAnswer: Branches of the basilar artery. The basilar artery gives off numerous pontine arteries that supply the pons, including the basilar artery itself running in the basilar groove on the anterior surface.

explanation: Pontine hemorrhage causes pinpoint pupils (due to sympathetic pathway damage), hyperpyrexia (due to hypothalamic dysfunction), and quadriplegia (due to corticospinal tract damage). The pons contains the descending sympathetic pathway and reticular formation.
keyConcept: Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia. Disrupts sympathetic pathways and corticospinal tracts.
modelAnswer: Pinpoint pupil (due to disruption of descending sympathetic pathways), hyperpyrexia (damage to hypothalamic temperature-regulating centers), and quadriplegia (bilateral corticospinal tract damage). Also may cause respiratory arrest and loss of consciousness.

explanation: The midbrain is supplied by branches from the posterior cerebral artery (main supply to the cerebral peduncles and colliculi) and the superior cerebellar artery (supplying the inferior colliculus and surrounding area).
keyConcept: Midbrain: branches of posterior cerebral artery and superior cerebellar artery.
modelAnswer: Branches of the posterior cerebral artery (supplies cerebral peduncles, red nucleus, substantia nigra, superior colliculus) and branches of the superior cerebellar artery (supplies inferior colliculus and adjacent midbrain).

explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (due to anterior spinal artery occlusion) causes: contralateral hemiplegia (corticospinal tract), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue paralysis (CN XII nucleus).
keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia + proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue paralysis.
modelAnswer: Contralateral flaccid hemiplegia (corticospinal tract), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral lower motor neuron paralysis of the tongue (hypoglossal nucleus damage).

explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome, usually from PICA occlusion) causes: ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss (spinal V nucleus), contralateral body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral palate/pharynx/larynx paralysis (nucleus ambiguus), loss of taste (solitary nucleus), and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (sympathetic chain).
keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg): ipsilateral face sensory loss, contralateral body sensory loss, ataxia, dysphagia, Horner's.
modelAnswer: Ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature from face (spinal nucleus of trigeminal), contralateral loss of pain and temperature from body (spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral paralysis of palate, pharynx and larynx (nucleus ambiguus), loss of taste sensation (solitary nucleus), and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (descending sympathetic tract).

explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures typically cause CSF rhinorrhea (cerebrospinal fluid leaking through nose), orbital hemorrhage, and subconjunctival ecchymosis (blood tracking into the orbit and around eyes).
keyConcept: Anterior cranial fossa fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, orbital hemorrhage, subconjunctival hemorrhage.
modelAnswer: Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea (CSF leak from nose due to meningeal tear), hemorrhage into the orbital cavity causing orbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), and subconjunctival hemorrhage. May also cause anosmia if olfactory nerves are damaged.

explanation: The four single (unpaired) dural venous sinuses are: superior sagittal sinus (in falx cerebri superiorly), inferior sagittal sinus (in falx cerebri inferiorly), straight sinus (confluence of falx and tentorium), and occipital sinus (in falx cerebelli).
keyConcept: Single sinuses: superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, occipital.
modelAnswer: Superior sagittal sinus (in upper border of falx cerebri), inferior sagittal sinus (in lower border of falx cerebri), straight sinus (junction of falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli), and occipital sinus (in falx cerebelli).

explanation: The six paired dural venous sinuses are: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, and transverse. These drain blood from the brain to the internal jugular vein via the sigmoid sinus.
keyConcept: Paired sinuses: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior/inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.
modelAnswer: Sphenoparietal sinus (along lesser wing of sphenoid), cavernous sinus (lateral to sella turcica), superior petrosal sinus (along petrous ridge), inferior petrosal sinus (below petrous ridge), sigmoid sinus (continuation to jugular bulb), and transverse sinus (in tentorium cerebelli).

explanation: The superior sagittal sinus receives: superior cerebral veins (draining the cerebral convexity), diploic veins (from skull bones), and arachnoid granulations ( CSF reabsorption). It ends at the confluence of sinuses.
keyConcept: Superior sagittal sinus tributaries: superior cerebral veins, diploic veins, arachnoid granulations.
modelAnswer: Superior cerebral veins (from the lateral surface of cerebral hemispheres), diploic veins (from the skull tables), and arachnoid granulations and villi (for CSF reabsorption into the venous system).

explanation: The cavernous sinus is a paired venous sinus on each side of the sella turcica. Its external relations include: anteriorly - superior orbital fissure; posteriorly - apex of petrous temporal and crus cerebri; medially - pituitary gland and sphenoid sinus; laterally - temporal lobe; superiorly - optic tract and ICA; inferiorly - foramen lacerum.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus relations: laterally = temporal lobe; medially = pituitary; anteriorly = superior orbital fissure; posteriorly = petrous apex.
modelAnswer: Anteriorly: superior orbital fissure and apex of orbit. Posteriorly: apex of petrous temporal bone and crus cerebri of midbrain. Medially: pituitary gland and sphenoidal air sinus. Laterally: temporal lobe of cerebrum. Superiorly: optic tract and internal carotid artery. Inferiorly: foramen lacerum.

explanation: The cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery (with its sympathetic plexus) and several cranial nerves: oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), maxillary division (V2), and abducent (VI).
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus contents: ICA, CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI. Important clinical relevance for cavernous sinus syndrome.
modelAnswer: Oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), maxillary nerve (CN V2), abducent nerve (CN VI), and the internal carotid artery (with its surrounding sympathetic plexus). These structures run in the lateral wall (nerves) and center (ICA) of the sinus.

explanation: The cavernous sinus receives blood from: superior ophthalmic vein (from orbit), inferior ophthalmic vein, central vein of retina, and superficial middle cerebral vein. These tributaries drain the orbit and cerebral surface.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus tributaries: superior/inferior ophthalmic veins, central retinal vein, superficial middle cerebral vein.
modelAnswer: Superior ophthalmic vein (draining the orbit and face), inferior ophthalmic vein, central vein of retina, and superficial middle cerebral vein (draining the cerebral cortex).

explanation: The cavernous sinus drains posteriorly via the superior petrosal sinus (to transverse-sigmoid sinus junction) and inferiorly via the inferior petrosal sinus (directly to internal jugular bulb).
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drainage: superior petrosal sinus → transverse-sigmoid; inferior petrosal sinus → internal jugular vein.
modelAnswer: Superior petrosal sinus (drains to transverse-sigmoid sinus junction) and inferior petrosal sinus (drains directly to internal jugular bulb). These connections allow blood to drain from the cavernous sinus to the systemic circulation.

explanation: The cavernous sinus communicates with: the pterygoid venous plexus (via emissary veins through foramen ovale), the facial vein (via superior ophthalmic vein), and the opposite cavernous sinus (via intercavernous sinuses).
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus communications: pterygoid plexus, facial vein (via ophthalmic), opposite cavernous sinus.
modelAnswer: Pterygoid venous plexus via emissary vein passing through foramen ovale, facial vein via superior ophthalmic vein, and the opposite cavernous sinus via the intercavernous sinuses. These connections explain spread of facial infections to cavernous sinus.

explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) consists of about 20 small filaments that pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach the olfactory bulb. These are actuallyaxons of bipolar olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal mucosa.
keyConcept: CN I (olfactory): 20 filaments through cribriform plate to olfactory bulb. Only cranial nerve without distinct nucleus.
modelAnswer: Olfactory nerve (CN I). The olfactory nerves consist of approximately 20 small nerve filaments that pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to synapse in the olfactory bulb on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe.

explanation: The optic nerve (CN II) passes through the optic canal, accompanied by the ophthalmic artery. The optic canal also transmits the central retinal artery (branch of ophthalmic). The nerve is actually a tract of the brain, not a typical peripheral nerve.
keyConcept: CN II (optic): through optic canal with ophthalmic artery. Actually CNS tissue, not peripheral nerve.
modelAnswer: Optic nerve (CN II). It passes through the optic canal along with the ophthalmic artery (branch of internal carotid). The central retinal artery (a branch of the ophthalmic artery) also passes through the optic canal with the nerve.
